challenges.name: percentiles-from-samples
challenges.title: What do these percentiles say?
challenges.description: Two pieces of evidence from CodeDev load tests: ten raw samples of the submit endpoint, and two runs of the leaderboard compared by mean and by p99. Decide which reading is right.

questions.question:
Ten successful requests to POST /api/submissions from a short smoke test, sorted by duration (ms):

180, 190, 195, 205, 210, 220, 240, 260, 300, 4100

The course uses nearest-rank percentiles: rank = ceil(p / 100 * n), value = the rank-th smallest sample.

Statement: "The p95 of these samples is 300 ms, so 95% of the submissions were accepted within 300 ms."
questions.explanation: False. With n = 10, rank = ceil(0.95 * 10) = ceil(9.5) = 10, so p95 is the 10th value: 4,100 ms. Only 9 of 10 requests (90%) finished within 300 ms; claiming 95% would need at least 9.5 of them. The common mistake is to round the rank down, or to use int(p / 100 * n) as a 0-based index without checking where it lands, and read the 9th value. It also shows a limit of small samples: with 10 samples, p95 and p99 are both simply the maximum, so a single slow request decides them. Report p99 only from a run with enough samples.

questions.question:
Two load test runs of GET /api/leaderboard, same load profile, 12,000 successful requests each, no failures:

run   change                                     mean     p50      p99
A     before                                     180 ms    62 ms   2,400 ms
B     400 ms timeout on the slow ranking query,  210 ms   175 ms     410 ms
      then a precomputed ranking table

Statement: "For learners, run B is better at the tail even though its mean is higher: in run B, 99% of the requests finished within 410 ms, against 2,400 ms in run A."
questions.explanation: True. The p99 is a statement about requests: in run B, at least 99% of the 12,000 requests (11,880 of them) took 410 ms or less, while in run A the slowest 1% took 2,400 ms or more. The mean mixes everything into one number: run A's many fast requests hide its slow ones, and in run B the typical request got slower (p50 175 ms) while the worst ones got much faster. The misconception is to compare runs by their mean: it can rise while the experience of the slowest learners improves a lot, and it can fall while it gets worse. Compare the percentiles you have a target for (here p95 and p99), with enough samples behind them.

challenges.name: percentiles-per-endpoint
challenges.title: Percentiles per endpoint from raw samples
challenges.description:
The weekly load test report of CodeDev shows one average per endpoint, and GET /api/leaderboard looks green at about 260 ms while some learners wait seconds for it. Replace the average with percentiles computed from the raw samples the load generator recorded, and keep the mean next to them so the gap is visible.

Input (stdin): {"samples": [...]}. Each sample is one request: {"endpoint": "GET /api/leaderboard", "ms": 64.9, "status": 200}. ms is the latency in milliseconds (at most one decimal); samples come in any order, endpoints mixed.

Write summarize(samples) (and the helper percentile(sorted_ms, p)). Rules:
- A sample is invalid when it is not an object, its endpoint is not a non-empty string, its ms is not a number or is below 0 (true and false are not numbers; 0 is valid), or its status is not an integer (true, false and "200" are not integers). Invalid samples are skipped and counted in invalid.
- A valid sample is successful when 200 <= status <= 399. Any other status is failed: 4xx, 5xx, and 0, which the generator records when no response arrived (timeout, connection error). Failed samples are counted in failed of their endpoint and never used in mean or percentiles: a 3 ms 503 is not a fast request.
- Percentiles are nearest-rank on the successful ms of one endpoint, sorted ascending: rank = ceil(p / 100 * n), value = sorted_ms[rank - 1], for p = 50, 95 and 99. They are values of real samples: not rounded, not interpolated.
- mean = round(sum of successful ms / count, 1) with Python's round.
- An endpoint with valid samples but no successful one has count 0 and mean, p50, p95, p99 null.

Output (stdout, printed by the runner): {"endpoints": [{"endpoint": ..., "count": successful, "failed": failed, "mean": ..., "p50": ..., "p95": ..., "p99": ...}, ...], "invalid": n}. One entry per endpoint that has at least one valid sample, sorted by endpoint name (Python's sorted on the strings). No samples -> {"endpoints": [], "invalid": 0}.

Example: samples of GET /api/me with ms 31.0, 29.5, 30.2, 250.0, 28.8, 30.9 (status 200) and 3.0 (status 503) give {"endpoint": "GET /api/me", "count": 6, "failed": 1, "mean": 66.7, "p50": 30.2, "p95": 250.0, "p99": 250.0}.

Constraints: Python 3 standard library only; up to a few thousand samples.
hints: If 10 learners loaded the leaderboard and you sort their times, which position must you read so that at least 95% of them waited no longer than that value? What do you do when 95% of 10 is not a whole number?

Look at three places: the rank (rounded up, and 1-based while Python lists are 0-based), the status check that decides whether a sample's ms belongs in the latency list at all, and the type checks (in Python, isinstance(True, int) is True).

A similar case on other data: five successful samples of GET /api/courses/:id, 120.4, 98.0, 101.5, 870.2, 99.9, plus a timeout (status 0). Sorted: 98.0, 99.9, 101.5, 120.4, 870.2 (n = 5; the timeout only adds 1 to failed). p50: rank = ceil(0.5 * 5) = 3 -> 101.5. p95: rank = ceil(4.75) = 5 -> 870.2. Mean: 1290.0 / 5 = 258.0, two and a half times the median.

tests.name: One endpoint: two slow requests pull the mean far above the median
Two endpoints, sorted by name; a 503 is counted as failed, not as a latency
Fast 503s, 429s and timeouts (status 0) stay out of the percentiles; all-failed endpoint: nulls
Invalid samples (wrong types, negative ms, missing fields, bool values) are skipped and counted
Rank boundaries: 1 sample, 20 samples (p95 = 19th value), 100 samples (p99 = 99th value)
Large: 1,200 shuffled samples over 3 endpoints with failures
